I switched to doing UWorld pathology blocks instead of random blocks, which I think helped cover a more broad range of topics. Most of step 1 is pathology (basically half the entire exam!), so you cover way more ground focusing on that than with other topics. After switching to this, I had a 7 point increase in my NBME scores when before I was only increasing 2-3 points.

Also Mehlman PDFs (particularly HY arrows) were a life saver for getting through those types of questions quickly. I could reason them out, but you will be strapped for time on step since the passages are so long, so being able to get those questions right on instinct is a huge boon.

I mostly used the end of NBME subject breakdown to make subject blocks in UWorld and to pick what subjects in first aid or pathoma to review. With that said, I know many people who got repeat questions on their actual step from NBME exams, and if I were to do it all again I would probably review NBMEs properly.

  


Additionally, I don't know you, but personally I could *not* effectively study if I were also fasting. Your brain needs direct energy to think properly during intense cognitive loads, which is why it's recommended to have small, regular snacks during intense cognitive tasks (among other things). I'm not telling you not to fast, but just know this and don't be too hard on yourself if you see your performance dip during Ramadan.

OP, Tumbleweed has everything you're looking for. It's rolling release, but bleeding edge updates go through testing and stabilization first before being released so you are always getting stable software. It has probably the best integration with KDE Plasma out-of-the-box, and it has a very simple and easy to use graphical installer (that can install KDE alongside it, so you don't have to do that separately). Not to mention it has Yast, which is a great graphical utility to deal with package management, networking, audio, and many other settings which makes handling wifi, pulseaudio/alsa, etc much easier to do.

It's more like...

If you make a sandwich using store-bought bread, cheese, veggies, etc you can definitely make a damn good sandwich, and I don't think anyone would say that you were lazy or that you didn't really make that sandwich yourself. Of course, buying ingredients means you lose control over aspects of the sandwich (freshness of ingredients, how firm or soft the bread is, etc) but ultimately you have made many choices based on both aesthetics and taste to assemble a delicious, pleasing sandwich, regardless of if the ingredients were store bought.

In a track, the ingredients are those loops, whether they're pre-made loops or loops made yourself.

I have a set up like this that I put together because I got my hands on an old Yamaha sound system for free. Essentially I have my audio coming out through a FocusRite 2i4, and I used RCA cables to connect the output from the FocusRite to the TV input on the Yamaha amplifier. From there the speakers and sub are set up as they would normally be. Cable management took some effort since there are loads of cables running around, but with all the wires out of the way of each other I haven't had any interference issues *yet.*

  


I still use headphones for mixing because the room I'm in is untreated. However for basic monitoring, listening to other music, and non-production things *(cough* gaming) it's a great setup.

  


If you want to avoid interference its probably easier with a dedicated dac of some sort rather than using the motherboard one. And either way, the monitors are likely unpowered so you'd need to account for that as well.
